sources.text: # tracon **Air traffic control for parallel Claude Code subagents.** A live terminal and browser monitor that spots stuck, blocked and drifting agents, and the worktree file conflicts headed for your merge. [![PyPI](https://img.shields.io/pypi/v/tracon)](https://pypi.org/project/tracon/) [![Python 3.12+](https://img.shields.io/pypi/pyversions/tracon)](https://pypi.org/project/tracon/) [![tests](https://github.com/phalladar/tracon/actions/workflows/test.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/phalladar/tracon/actions/workflows/test.yml) [![MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/license-MIT-blue)](LICENSE) ![A terminal split in two. On the left, a Claude Code session is asked to /expedite checkout-v2 and dispatches seven worktree agents. On the right, tracon lists them as they start; over the run one agent is blocked on a permission prompt, one goes idle, one drifts off its brief and one is stuck retrying a failing command. The user selects the stuck agent in tracon, presses n to nudge the lead with a drafted note; it arrives in the Claude Code session, the lead messages the agent, and tracon shows it back on track.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phalladar/tracon/main/docs/screenshots/hero.gif) Left: a Claude Code session orchestrating seven worktree agents. Right: tracon in a split next to it. A made-up run from tracon --demo , sped up. ```sh uvx tracon --demo # look around a made-up run; no Claude Code session needed uvx tracon # watch the Claude Code session in the next split, else your newest with subagents ``` You dispatched six agents an hour ago. One has been waiting 40 minutes on a permission prompt nobody can see. Two are editing `shop/cart.py` at the same time. One is restyling the admin pages its brief said to leave alone, and another has run the same failing command six times. Claude Code's status line shows none of it. Like a [TRACON](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terminal_radar_approach_control_facilities) controller watching every aircraft on one scope, `tracon` shows every agent at once: what it is doing, whether it is holding, whether it has drifted off its brief, and whether two of them are on a collision course in the same file. Run it in a split next to your session. - **Read-only and local.** It reads the transcripts Claude Code already writes to disk and never writes to your repository. It sends something to a session only when you press `n`. See [What it touches](#what-it-touches). - **No setup.** No hooks, no config, no account. Start it in a split next to your session and it finds that session. - **Optional LLM judge.** A small model checks each busy agent against its brief, for about a tenth of a cent a check, with a hard per-run budget. `--no-judge` turns it off. > tracon is an independent project. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by or sponsored by > Anthropic. "Claude" and "Claude Code" are trademarks of Anthropic. ## What it catches ### Every agent on one scope Agents waiting on a permission prompt nobody can answer, agents that went quiet, hung test runs, processes left behind, loops, edits to the wrong checkout or on a stale base, two agents changing the same file, and (with the optional [judge](#the-judge-optional-on-by-default)) agents drifting from their brief. Red needs you now; amber is worth a look. ![tracon's terminal view: a table of agents with states BLOCKED, IDLE, RUNNING and WORKING, judge verdicts on track, drifting and stuck, and flags such as LOOP, COLLIDE and STALE-BASE; below it, the selected agent's feed of repeated connection-refused errors](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phalladar/tracon/main/docs/screenshots/tui-overview.png) ### Why one is in trouble `enter` opens an agent: what it is doing, the judge's concern and how the verdict changed, every flag explained, the files it touched outside its brief, and a live tail of what it said, in full. The tool calls between two messages fold into one line (`▸ 23 tool calls Read 5 · Edit 8 …`); click it to open that run, or press `e` to open them all. The brief and the lead's messages show three lines; click `▸ N more lines` to read the rest. ![tracon's detail view of an agent the judge marks as drifting: it has edited admin files its brief says to leave alone](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phalladar/tracon/main/docs/screenshots/tui-detail.png) ### Merge conflicts before the merge `x` shows which agent edited which file. `!` marks a file two agents were editing at the same time. ![tracon's files heatmap: rows of files, one column per agent, with two agents both editing shop/cart.py marked with an exclamation mark](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phalladar/tracon/main/docs/screenshots/tui-files.png) ### Nudge the lead in one key `n` nudges your orchestrating session about the selected agent: tracon drafts a note with the agent's state, flags, the judge's concern and what to do, and sends it straight away (see [Nudging the lead](#nudging-the-lead)). ### Replay the whole run `t` is the timeline. `[` and `]` rewind and forward, `space` plays it back, and `--at "07:20"` opens any past session as it stood at that time. ![tracon's terminal timeline: one row per agent, coloured by edits, shell calls and reads, with silent stretches dotted](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phalladar/tracon/main/docs/screenshots/tui-timeline.png) [Reading the screen](#reading-the-screen) lists every state and flag, what it means, and what to do about it. With `--notify`, a desktop notification fires when an agent needs you. The terminal title is set to the watched session's name (`◎ `, mirroring Claude Code's `✳ `), so the split reads as part of that session. ## Install Requires Python 3.12+, on macOS or Linux. ```sh uv tool install tracon # or: pipx install tracon uv tool install 'tracon[api]' # optional: judge through the Anthropic API instead of `claude -p` ``` Or run it without installing: `uvx tracon`. From source: ```sh git clone https://github.com/phalladar/tracon && cd tracon uv tool install --editable . ``` ## Use ```sh cd your-project && tracon # the session in the next split, else the newest in this project (or anywhere) tracon --demo # a made-up run, to look around tracon web # browser view only tracon --list # recent sessions that spawned subagents tracon -s 4f2a # pick a session by id prefix tracon --at "2026-10-11 07:20" # replay a session as it stood at that time tracon --once # print one snapshot and exit tracon --once --json # snapshot as JSON (for scripts and status bars) ``` A good layout: your orchestrating session on one side, `tracon` in a split next to it (in Ghostty, `cmd+d`). Without `--session`, tracon picks, in order: 1. the Claude Code session in a split of the same tab (Ghostty 1.3+ on macOS), matched by the name Claude Code gives its terminal, even before it has started any subagents; 2. the newest session with subagents in this folder's project, or in the nearest parent folder that has one; 3. the newest session with subagents anywhere. It keeps checking: when the session in the next split changes, or a new session with subagents takes the top spot, tracon switches to it. Picking a session with `s` stops that. ### Terminal keys | Key | | |---|---| | `enter` | agent detail: state, judge verdict, flags, files, live processes, and what the agent said, with the lead's messages and its tool calls folded between them (`e` or a click unfolds them) | | `e` | open or fold every run of tool calls and every long brief or lead message, in the pane under the table and in the detail (a click on `▸` does one) | | `t` | timeline: every agent across the run, coloured by activity, with the lead's merges and messages | | `x` | files heatmap: which agents edited which files, concurrent edits marked `!` | | `w` | open the browser view | | `j` | ask the judge about the selected agent now | | `d` | dismiss the judge's drifting or stuck verdict on the selected agent (press again to restore) | | `n` | nudge the lead about the selected agent: sends a note with its state, flags and what to do (live only) | | `[` `]` / `{` `}` | rewind / forward 5 / 30 min (enters replay) · `space` play · `l` back to live | | `o` / `c` | open the agent's worktree in a new terminal window (Ghostty if installed) / copy its path | | `s` | sessions, last active first: pick one to watch (stops following the next split and new sessions) | | `h` / `q` | hide finished agents / quit | ### Browser view `w` in the terminal, or `tracon web`, serves a page on `127.0.0.1`: ![The tracon browser timeline replaying a run: seven subagents spawn and work, coloured by edits, shell calls and reads, with judge verdicts per agent and the lead's merges and messages along the top](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/phalladar/tracon/main/docs/screenshots/replay.gif) - **Timeline**: zoom with the scroll wheel, drag to pan, double-click to fit. Hover any bar for the calls it covers. Silent stretches past the idle threshold are drawn in orange. - **Files**: heatmap of edits per file per agent, shared files first. - **Replay scrubber**: drag through the run, or press ▶ to play it back. - Click an agent for its detail drawer and live activity feed. ## Reading the screen Each agent row has a **state** (what it is doing now), a **JUDGE** column (the LLM's read of whether it is on brief), and any number of **flags** (things worth a look). Press `enter` on a row for the detail, which shows the judge's one-line concern and every flag's explanation. You don't control agents from tracon; it is read-only. When something needs action, you act in your orchestrating session: answer the prompt there, or ask the lead to message, stop or re-dispatch the agent. ### Columns | Column | Shows | |---|---| | **STATE** | What it is doing now (below) | | **TASK** | The description the lead gave the agent; the pinned row is the lead itself | | **MODEL** | The model it runs on | | **JUDGE** | The judge's latest verdict (below) | | **NOW** | Its current or latest action | | **QUIET** | Time since its transcript last moved; red past the 5 min idle threshold | | **RUN** | Time since it started | | **CONTEXT** | Context size in tokens; amber above 300k, red above 450k | | **EDITS** | Files it edited; `(n⚑)` counts those the brief never names | | **COMMITS** | `git commit` calls it made | | **MSGS** | Messages the lead sent it | | **FLAGS** | Things worth a look (below) | ### Colours | Colour | Browser label | Means | |---|---|---| | red | Needs you | act now: the agent can't continue, or is doing damage | | amber | Check | have a look when you can; often fine | | green | Working | nothing to do | | grey | Done / Note | finished, or history kept for context | Once an agent has finished, its flags turn grey: they are history, not action. Only **OUTSIDE** and **ORPHAN** stay loud, because what they describe outlives the agent. ### States | State | Means | What to do | |---|---|---| | **BLOCKED** | An instant call (Edit, Read, `git status`) has been open for 45 s, or a shell call with nothing running: it is waiting on a permission prompt | Answer the prompt if it is showing in your session. If nobody can see it, allow that tool in your permission settings, or have the lead stop and re-dispatch the agent | | **IDLE** | No transcript activity for 5 min and nothing running | Check the last lines of its feed: it often hit an error or is waiting for input it will never get. Have the lead message it or stop it | | **STALLED** | A process has run for 20 min with no file change or commit | Usually a hung test or a watcher that never exits. Check the process in the detail; kill it, or have the lead stop the agent | | **ORPHANED** | Silent, but a detached process it started is still running after its parent died | Kill the process (pid in the detail) | | **WAITING** | Its turn has ended (or it is quiet) while background work it launched still runs | Usually nothing: it resumes when that work finishes. If the work is stuck, see STALLED | | **PENDING** | Replay only: a tool call was open, and without process data tracon can't tell a long run from a prompt | Nothing; go live to see which it is | | **RUNNING** | A tool call is in progress (a build, a test run) | Nothing | | **WORKING** | Making calls normally | Nothing | | **STARTING** | Dispatched, no activity yet | Nothing | | **DONE** | Finished: handed back a report, the lead was told it completed, or it ended with a final answer and nothing running | Read its report; merge | | **STOPPED** | Stopped by the lead, failed, or killed | Check why if you didn't expect it | A pinned **◆ lead** row shows the orchestrating session itself (running, working, or waiting on its agents or on you), so its activity is never mistaken for a subagent's. ### Flags | Flag | Means | What to do | |---|---|---| | **LOOP** | The same call 3× in a row with no edit in between | It is spinning. Have the lead tell it what it is missing, or stop it | | **ERRORS** | Its last 3 tool calls failed | Look at the errors in the feed; it may recover on its own | | **DENIED** | Tool calls were denied, with the classifier's reasons (e.g. "Modify Shared Resources"), or refused by a guard (Claude Code's worktree isolation or its sleep block, which say what to do instead). A denial is amber for 30 min, then grey. A guard refusal stays grey while the agent's next call gets through, and turns amber only when it is refused twice in a row | For a denial, decide whether it should have that permission; if so, allow it and have the lead tell it to retry. For an amber refusal, have the lead tell it to do what the refusal says, or to report what it can't do | | **OUTSIDE** | A worktree agent edited the main checkout instead of its worktree | Check `git status` in your main checkout and undo or move those edits | | **BRANCH** | Its worktree is on a different branch from the one it was given | Check it hasn't committed to the wrong branch before you merge | | **STALE-BASE** | It started editing before merging the base branch, after the lead had already merged something. Live, git has the last word: no flag once its HEAD contains the base, and the flag says how many commits behind it is | Expect conflicts; have it merge the base before it goes further | | **COLLIDE** | Another agent edited the same file while both were running. Press `x` for the heatmap | The second merge may conflict. Decide which agent owns the file, or plan the merge order | | **OFF-BRIEF** | It edited files the brief never names (grey: often legitimate) | Glance at the list; worth a question only if the files look unrelated | | **BG** | It launched background or detached runs. Amber when its brief says to run in the foreground and nowhere allows a background or `nohup` run | If amber, it is ignoring the brief; have the lead remind it | | **UNCOMMITTED** | Edits left uncommitted for 45 min | Work at risk if the worktree is cleaned up; have it commit | | **CTX** | Context above 300k (amber) or 450k (red) tokens | It will slow down and forget earlier instructions. Have it wrap up and hand back, or re-dispatch the rest fresh | | **ORPHAN** | A detached process is still running from its worktree. Grey while the agent is still working (usually it is polling its own `nohup` run); red once the agent goes quiet or finishes | Kill it once you're sure nothing needs it | | **DRIFT** | The judge says it is drifting (below), and you haven't dismissed it | See below | | **STUCK** | The judge says it is stuck (below), and you haven't dismissed it | See below | ### Judge verdicts The **JUDGE** column shows the latest verdict from the optional [LLM check](#the-judge-optional-on-by-default). It is a small model's opinion of the brief against the last 40 actions, so treat it as a prompt to look, not a fact. The detail view (`enter`) shows what the agent is doing, the judge's concern, and how the verdict has changed over time. | Verdict | Means | What to do | |---|---|---| | ✓ **on track** | Its recent actions serve the brief's steps, even if slowly | Nothing | | ↯ **drifting** (amber, adds **DRIFT**) | It is doing work the brief doesn't ask for, widening scope, or breaking a rule the brief states (running tests in the background when told to run them in the foreground, editing files it was told not to touch). The concern names an action it can see; growth that still serves the brief, or a baseline taken on the base branch, doesn't count | Read the concern in the detail. If it is real, have the lead message the agent to get back to the brief, or stop it. If the extra work is fine (your brief was narrower than you meant), have the lead tell the agent so with `SendMessage`: the judge treats the lead's messages as part of the brief and checks again after the agent's next action. If it is a false alarm, press `d` to dismiss it | | ⟳ **stuck** (red, adds **STUCK**) | It repeats actions without progress, retries a failure without changing approach, or waits on something that won't come | Find the repeated failure in the feed. Give it the missing piece through the lead, or stop it and re-dispatch with a better brief. If it is a false alarm, press `d` to dismiss it | | ? **unclear** | Too little activity to tell | Nothing; wait | | … **judging** | A check is in progress | Nothing | | blank | Not judged yet (it needs 5 tool calls), or the judge is off | Nothing | Verdicts refresh at most every 3 min per agent, after 5 more tool calls. Press `j` to re-check the selected agent now, for example after the lead has nudged it. Finished agents are never judged; their last verdict stays, greyed out, and DRIFT and STUCK are dropped. **Dismissing.** `d` on a drifting or stuck agent marks that verdict as dismissed: it shows greyed out as "· dismissed", DRIFT or STUCK goes away, the nudge leaves the concern out, and the next check lists it to the judge as a concern you've cleared, so it shouldn't be raised again on the same actions. A new concern flags as usual. `d` again restores the verdict. ## The judge (optional, on by default) Rules cat

sources.text: Show HN: Tracon (air traffic control for subagents) | Hacker News Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login Show HN: Tracon (air traffic control for subagents) ( github.com/phalladar ) 1 point by allocate 2 hours ago | hide | past | favorite | discuss My Claude Code workflow usually involves... a lot of subagents. I make one Opus model coordinate work as my tech lead, it dispatches subagents using models appropriate for the task into their own git worktrees, and then I try to multitask and do something else while they run. I'd been finding lately (particularly with Opus 5.5) that there was a ton of drift and instances of subagents not doing anything and it was evading the attention of the TL despite the instructions I gave it to have them report in at a regular cadence. Running tracon in a split terminal is my new personal workflow. It gives me early indicators when things start going off the rails (ex. blocked on a prompt, idle, looping on a failing command, simultaneous edits to files other subagents are editing, drifting off the brief, etc.) and I can interrogate the subagent's workflow and by pressing n the main agent gets a note to make a call on how and if to correct it. Read-only and runs on your machine: it tails transcripts in ~/.claude/projects/ and checks each worktree with ps, lsof, and git -- only thing that leaves your machine is what the Haiku judge reads for classification (or optionally you can turn that off with --no-judge). I've found it super useful for the game I'm building and figured others in the community might also find it useful. If you just want to give it a spin without committing: uvx tracon --demo macOS and Linux, Python 3.12+, MIT. (Not affiliated with Anthropic.) help Consider applying for YC's Winter 2027 batch! Multiple projects. Works with anything. Your own tools, AI-built projects or open source software you found online. It doesn’t matter, PanelAlpha Engine just runs it. AI works through Engine, not directly on the server. A clear structure. Projects, accounts and domains, all stay organized. Project isolation. Each runs separately in its own Docker container. Read more AI agent your server n8n WordPress Static site Your app Everything you need for production, out of the box. Deploy is only the beginning. PanelAlpha Engine is built for ongoing management, maintenance and professional production workflows. See it online right away. Every deploy gets a temporary URL you can open, test and share immediately. Add a password when you need it. Get me a preview link with password. Preview available at bingo.panelalpha.online. Backups (internal and external), SSL, FTP, SFTP, domains, databases, CRON and logs are already there for you and your agent. Roll back to yesterday’s backup. Done. I restored yesterday’s backup and saved the current state just in case. Every project gets its own safe space. Docker isolation, firewall and ModSecurity/OWASP WAF rules with only the ports it needs open. One broken app can’t take the others down. Only let our office access this internal tool. I updated the firewall so it’s only accessible from your office IP 83.24.11.5 . Easy Cloudflare connection. Connect your account once and use DNS, tunnels and caching across your projects. Set up a Cloudflare Tunnel for this project through n8n.mydomain.com. Done. Tunnel active at n8n.mydomain.com. Explore Full Capabilities 4 years of PanelAlpha. 8,000 active sites. Privately owned. PanelAlpha started in 2022 as a WordPress management platform for hosting providers and agencies, now managing around 8,000 active sites across 60+ partners. We are part of INBS.Software, with 15 years in hosting and 40,000+ customers across our products. We’re privately owned and plan to stay that way. PanelAlpha Engine FAQ Everything you need to know before installing Engine and putting your first project online. Need more help? Join us on Discord Why do I even need PanelAlpha Engine? Building projects with AI is fun. Running them on your own server usually isn’t. Most self-hosted tools are still technical and expect you to know your way around DevOps. PanelAlpha Engine changes that. Connect it to your AI and let it handle the deployment, setup and day-to-day management for you, inside a safe, controlled environment. You get the benefits of self-hosting without having to become a sysadmin or worry about AI making a mess of your server. Do I need my own server? Yes, PanelAlpha Engine has been created as a tool for AI agents to manage your own servers. This means that you need to have a server, potentially a VPS, to run it. Perhaps in the future we will also simplify the process of buying servers, so you won’t even have to run an install command. Which AI agents work with PanelAlpha Engine? You can connect pretty much any AI agent that works with an MCP server. We specifically provided an explanation of how to use it with the most popular ones in our Documentation: Connecting AI Agent to PanelAlpha Engine What projects can I deploy with PanelAlpha Engine? Our primary objective for PanelAlpha Engine is to make it a universal tool for ANY project. Whether it’s a static site, WordPress, a front-end or back-end solution, it should work. What is reported if a deploy fails? In order to make PanelAlpha Engine support “any project”, we need to make sure that we get information about the errors you are facing and can potentially reproduce them on our end. PanelAlpha Engine collects data about the technology stack and repository that you are using (only if it’s public!). PanelAlpha Engine prepares a report that you can preview yourself, and it does not send any content from your project files to our servers. You can always opt out of reporting, just keep in mind that we won’t even know that you have an issue and we won’t be able to solve it unless someone else faces the same problem. Whether its context window or application memory that's grinding to a halt, Subworkflow.ai is one approach to keep you going. Subworkflow.ai is a third party API service to help AI developers work with documents too large for context windows and runtime memory. Prequisites You'll need a Subworkflow.ai API key to use the Subworkflow.ai service. Add the API key as a header auth credential. More details in the official docs https://docs.subworkflow.ai/category/api-reference How it Works Import your document into your n8n workflow Upload it to the Subworkflow.ai service via the Extract API using the HTTP node. This endpoint takes files up to 100mb. Once uploaded, this will trigger an Extract job on the service's side and the response is a "job" record to track progress. Poll Subworkflow.ai 's Jobs endpoint and keep polling until the job is finished. You can use the "IF" node looping back unto itself to achieve this in n8n. Once the job is done, the Dataset of the uploaded document is ready for retrieval. Use the Datasets and DatasetItems API to retrieve whatever you need to complete your AI task. In this example, all pages are retrieved and run through a multimodal LLM to parse into markdown. A well-known process when parsing data tables or graphics are required. How to use Integrate Subworkflow's Extract API seemlessly into your existing document workflows to support larger documents from 100mb+ to up to 5000 pages. Customising the workflow Sometimes you don't want the entire document back especially if the document is quite large (think 500+ pages!), instead, use query parameters on the DatasetItems API to pick individual pages or a range of pages to reduce the load. Add optional keys inside the app. **[→ Quick Start](#-quick-start)** --- **[Quick Start](#-quick-start) · [First Five Minutes](#-the-first-five-minutes) · [Talk to It](#-talk-to-it) · [What's Live](#-whats-on-the-globe) · [Under the Hood](#-under-the-hood) · [Keys & Costs](#-api-keys) · [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md)** --- ## 🌍 Why This Exists God's Eye View brings public signals into one explorable globe. Track the world live. Talk to it. Break it. Extend it. Flight transponders, ship beacons, orbital elements, seismographs, and public cameras already tell us a lot about the world. God's Eye View puts them in the same place, so you can move between a global picture and an individual aircraft, ship, or street. It runs locally in your browser, with source code you can inspect and extend. > Half the magic is that it looks like a forbidden cockpit. The other half is that every line of code is inspectable. Most feeds are live or regularly refreshed. Traffic is simulated along real roads using aggregate location data. CCTV camera poses and rocket launch trajectories are coarse estimates. Start with the included data sources, then add your own. Each layer is a separate module. --- ## 🎛️ What This Thing Does - **🛩️ Cockpit view:** Ride inside a tracked flight — the camera holds the terrain under you all the way down. - **📡 Contacts:** A 250 km roster of everything near your target — step through live aircraft and drop into any cockpit. - **🎯 Click-to-track anything:** Camera locks on, draws a fading trail, surfaces full metadata — and a tracked fire or vessel hands you off to the nearest live camera in one click. - **🖊️ Voice whiteboard:** Speak annotations onto the world — real boundary polygons, marks, and routes. - **🛫 3D hangar:** Real per-class aircraft models — 787, ATR-72, Citation, Bell 206, MQ-9 — and a tracked contact swaps from glyph to 3D model as you close in. - **🎨 Reskin reality:** GLSL sensor looks over the normal globe — CRT, NVG, FLIR/thermal, Noir, Snow. - **🟩 Detection overlay:** Screen-space bounding boxes and IDs on everything in view. - **🎖️ Military HUD:** Tactical heads-up display with intelligence-style telemetry. - **🌐 Global Context:** Stage the full situational picture with one switch — and get your exact view back when you leave. - **🎥 Scene director:** Capture cinematic camera tours for clips and demos. - **🔗 Share Links:** Camera, style, layers, and even one tracked target serialize into a URL — a live target is a handoff, not a bookmark. - **🏠 Reset Globe:** One control — or one sentence — back to the full Earth. - **🌦️ Weather:** Animate GFS or ECMWF forecast wind, replay observed radar, satellite clouds and lightning on one timeline, and follow NHC/CPHC cyclone tracks. No key needed. - **📷 Mapped ALPR cameras:** License-plate-reader camera locations tagged in OpenStreetMap, one city at a time. Locations and tags only; no key needed. - **🔭 Satellite passes:** Ask by voice when any loaded satellite next rises over you: rise, peak and set times, and whether you can see it. - **🔎 Analyst answers:** Count, filter and rank satellites, datacenters and dams by voice, alongside flights, ships, fires and quakes; answers say when a feed is stale or on a fallback. - **🧭 Tilt and North Up:** Switch between straight-down and a 35° oblique, or put north at the top, while a tracked target stays centered. - **🔍 Keyless search:** Type coordinates or a bundled city or landmark to fly there with no network request; other names use Google when configured, then Photon and Nominatim. - **📦 Shareable scenes:** Import, preview and share Director scenes as files or bundles, with camera anchors, authored moves and data packs. - **🌊 Nepal flood scene:** Replay the Bhote Koshi flood: flood path, witness sources and before-and-after imagery (bundled data is non-commercial; see [DATA_SOURCES.md](DATA_SOURCES.md)). --- [![YouTube video about the God's Eye View open source release](https://img.youtube.com/vi/GRJaKcXZS94/maxresdefault.jpg)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GRJaKcXZS94) ▶️ **[The full walkthrough of everything below, on YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GRJaKcXZS94)** ## ⚡ Quick Start **Start without an account or API keys.** Both paths open the same app with Esri satellite imagery and keyless terrain. OSM is the fallback if Esri is unreachable. Flights, military traffic, satellites, earthquakes, public cameras, radio, and launches are available without keys. For photorealistic 3D, add a **Cesium ion token** for eligible personal, non-commercial use, or a **Google Maps key** for the direct, metered route and Google place search. Provider terms and quotas apply. Add keys through the app's **POWER UP** panel; [Keys & Costs](#-api-keys) explains the options. > **Already installed?** Update to the latest version. Older versions query > public OpenStreetMap Overpass servers, which now refuse them, so Traffic, > Mapped Installations and ALPR stay empty until you update. ### Path 1 — One click, no terminal 1. Install or update [Pinokio](https://desktop.pinokio.co/) to **8.2 or later**. 2. Open [God's Eye View in Pinokio](https://pinokio.co/apps/github-com-bilawalsidhu-gods-eye-view). 3. Click **Install**, then **Start**. Available on **Windows, macOS, and Linux**. The Pinokio maintainer reports cross-platform testing of the fixed installer. The launcher installs the locked dependencies, finds a free local port, and opens the app. **Tried before and installation failed?** Update Pinokio and try again. Version 8.2 fixes the launcher installation issue; [details from the Pinokio maintainer](https://pinokio.co/posts/01m1m4p9xxm3qw7dnnpj2wr93g). ### Path 2 — Terminal / coding agent Use **Node.js 24.x (24.14.0 or later) or 26.x**. The setup doctor warns about Node 25, which is end-of-life. ```bash git clone https://github.com/bilawalsidhu/gods-eye-view.git cd gods-eye-view npm ci npm run doctor npm run dev ``` Open **`http://localhost:4173`**. Choose **Live Contacts**, **Space Missions**, **Environmental**, or **Explore Manually** from the first-run panel. Startup performance A point-in-time M5/Chrome capture measured a median 1.86-second cold start. This is a comparison baseline, not a guarantee for your machine or connection. See [docs/PERFORMANCE.md](docs/PERFORMANCE.md). **macOS shortcut:** `./scripts/dev-fresh.sh` clears the Vite cache and pulls any configured keys straight from the Keychain. It starts keyless too. ### Then power it up — in the app, not in a file Keys are upgrades, not prerequisites. When you want one, click the **POWER UP** chip in the bottom-right corner: Provider Settings lists every supported key, what it switches on, and where to get it. Paste, hit **SAVE KEYS**, and the app restarts itself with the new capability on. Once everything is configured the chip reads **POWERED UP** — and if a compact layout hides it, `?setup=1` reopens the same panel. - **Where keys land:** Pinokio → the app's ignored `pinokio/ENVIRONMENT`; a terminal clone → the repo-root `.env`. Either file is made owner-only _before_ a secret is written into it. These are local plaintext files, excluded from Git; the app uses your keys to contact the providers. - **Keys you already have stay yours:** values from your shell or the macOS Keychain show as _configured externally_ and are read-only to the panel. - **What to get first:** the free [Cesium ion](https://cesium.com/ion) token (eligible personal, non-commercial use; current terms and quotas apply) for photorealistic 3D and world terrain; a Google Maps key only for the billing-enabled, metered route + Google place search; OpenAI when you want to talk to the world. Full map, costs included, in [Keys & Costs](#-api-keys). Older Pinokio versions and credential storage Do not enter credentials in Pinokio 8.0.40's native **Configure** panel: that release does not save this nested app file correctly, and it logs submitted values. Use **POWER UP → Provider Settings** inside GEV instead. The Pinokio 8.2 announcement fixes installation; it does not establish that this separate Configure issue is resolved. On macOS, the Keychain via `./scripts/dev-fresh.sh` remains the stronger storage option. The server binds to **localhost** on both paths, and Provider Settings answers requests only from your machine. Browser-side keys (Google Maps, Cesium ion) must be restricted at their providers — [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md) shows how, and it carries the LAN-sharing rules alongside [Keys & Costs](#-api-keys). --- ## 🕐 The First Five Minutes Choose a first-run mission, or try these in order. The GIFs show Google Photorealistic 3D; your starting basemap depends on the keys you've added. 1. **Light up the sky.** Take the **Live Contacts** mission (or turn on **Flights** yourself) — thousands of live aircraft, gliding on real telemetry, detection mesh already reading the scene. Click one: the camera locks on, a trail draws behind it, and its live telemetry card comes up. 2. **Take the controls.** Hit **COCKPIT** on your tracked plane and ride it down, switching sensors mid-flight: NVG into Ironbow FLIR. ![Riding with a live aircraft in cockpit view while switching sensor modes](docs/media/06-cockpit-ar.gif) 3. **Drop into a busy airport.** Search one and descend to the taxiways with **3D** aircraft on — grounded contacts, taxi trails, the whole apron working in real time. ![Moving from a full airport overhead down to close taxiway inspection with 3D flight models](docs/media/start-here/airport-ground-traffic-google-3d.gif) 4. **Look through a public camera.** Turn on **Cameras** over Austin, London, California, Finland, or Delaware (live video). The feeds aren't webcam embeds — they project _into_ the 3D city. Cycle coverage to **VIEWSHED** and every camera draws its estimated coverage volume — where it reaches, and where it goes blind. ![Diving into an Austin intersection with a live public camera projected into the 3D scene](docs/media/03-austin-cctv.gif) 5. **Track something in orbit.** Turn on **Satellites** and click the ISS — you ride along at orbital distance, orbit ring and all. ![Tracking the ISS along its orbital path as it crosses over Ukraine](docs/media/14-iss-over-ukraine.gif) 6. **Switch the optics.** Tap `1`–`7` — CRT, NVG, FLIR — and the whole live planet re-renders through a different sensor. ![Cycling a dense live globe through CRT, FLIR, and NVG in one continuous view](docs/media/01-style-sweep.gif) 7. **Talk to it** _(needs an OpenAI key)_: _"Take me to LAX and select the nearest airborne aircraft."_ 8. **Come home.** Hit **Reset Globe** — or just say _"zoom out to a globe view."_ **Keyboard:** `1`–`7` visual styles · `H` HUD · `D` detection · `C` cockpit · `` ` `` frame rate · `Esc` out. Trackpad pinch zooms the globe. --- ## 🛩️ The Cockpit > Every plane should let you do this. Real-time cockpit mode, built from live flight data: the camera rides your contact with real terrain holding underneath, all the way down — sensor styles come along for the ride, and **Contacts** keeps the 250 km roster one click away: jump plane to plane and fall straight into the next cockpit. ![Jumping between live aircraft and falling straight into a cockpit view](docs/media/12-switch-aircraft-cockpit.gif) The cockpit even carries its own briefing strip: nearby live signals, regional headlines, and real local weather — with an opt-in **WX** mode that renders volumetric clouds from actual observations around your aircraft. ![A live military contact ridden through Normal, NVG, and Ironbow FLIR with dense detection](docs/media/start-here/military-cockpit-dense-google-3d.gif) _Why cockpit mode exists: you're riding a real aircraft over real terrain — and you get to pick which sensor you see the world through._ --- ## 🎙️ Talk to It > Voice can use an **OpenAI API key** or, on the same machine, an opt-in signed-in **ChatGPT/Codex OAuth** session. The API-key path remains the default. Selecting ChatGPT OAuth in Provider Settings reuses an existing local sign-in or starts the Codex browser sign-in flow and selects OAuth when it completes. The OpenAI key still drives the **AI HUD summary**: a terse, five-word intelligence-style readout of the current view that regenerates as you move. The OAuth option is experimental. OpenAI documents ChatGPT plan usage for the [Responses API](https://developers.openai.com/siwc/token-sharing-open-source/models-and-inference); a supported third-party Realtime contract for reusing Codex tokens has not been confirmed. A successful token mint does not establish billing or support terms. GEV reads Codex's file credentials but does not write or refresh them. It checks token shape and expiry, and reports expired sign-in as requiring re-authentication. The login button runs `codex login`, permits one pending attempt, and reports exit failures or a two-minute timeout. `CODEX_HOME` must match the directory that Codex uses. If `CODEX_AUTH_JSON` points elsewhere, sign in separately or fix that mismatch before using the button. Codex credential storage must use `auth.json`; Keychain-only and in-memory storage are not readable by GEV. On Windows, the login button may not be able to start an npm-installed Codex; run `codex login` yourself, then select OAuth. See [Codex credential storage](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/auth#credential-storage). For a live voice check, run `node scripts/qa-voice-auth.mjs http://127.0.0.1:4189 oauth microphone.wav` against your local dev server. Use a WAV with three seconds of leading silence followed by a short spoken reply request. Replace `oauth` with `api-key` to check the API-key path. The check verifies audio input, a completed spoken reply, usage, resource cleanup, and reconnect. It saves screenshots and credential-free results under `.gev-logs/voice-auth/`. Click **GEV MIC**, grant the microphone, and just talk. This is more than a voice-controlled remote: - **🧠 It knows what it's looking at.** The agent pulls live scene context before answering — including coordinates, street names, active layers, and view scale. Ask _"what city is this?"_ mid-flight and it knows. - **🎯 Entity Q&A.** Click any plane, ship, or datacenter and ask _"what's this?"_ It answers using the object's live telemetry. - **👁️ Visual grounding.** At street level, it reads a viewport screenshot to identify legible signage and building names, and is instructed never to hallucinate labels. - **🎬 Cinematic framing.** _"Show me the planes overhead"_ pulls the camera back, angles it, and frames the live traffic like a director. - **🔒 Honest and secure.** The agent only confirms actions that succeeded. Your `OPENAI_API_KEY` never touches the browser; the client only gets a short-lived session token. If you choose **USE CHATGPT OAUTH** in Provider Settings, the local server uses that sign-in only to mint the same kind of short-lived Realtime credential, and refuses the OAuth path for non-loopback clients. Thirty tools, four jobs — the commands below come straight from the product's voice test suite and tool playbook: **🎥 Direct it** — drone-operator camera verbs: > 🗣️ _"Take me to Tokyo."_ · _"Orbit around this area slowly."_ · _"Draw the walking route from the Capitol to Zilker Park."_ → _"Fly the route we just drew."_ · _"Zoom out to a globe view."_ **🖊️ Annotate it** — a whiteboard over the real world: > 🗣️ _"Outline the state of Texas."_ · _"Annotate the Texas State Capitol and its grounds"_ — it draws the **actual enclosing boundary**, not a circle. · _"How far is the Eiffel Tower from the Louvre?"_ — a connector arrow appears and it speaks the distance. Everything persists until you say _"clear the map."_ **✍️ Or draw it yourself** — DISPLAY ▸ **Draw**: pick Area, Line or Pin, click the vertices on the real world, double-click to finish, label it. Same whiteboard, same persistence, no microphone needed. ![Zilker Park and Lady Bird Lake drawing onto the 3D city as persistent vector annotations, by voice](docs/media/01-voice-annotate-zilker.gif) ![A spoken distance measurement spanning an airport, inspected from orbit](docs/media/04-airport-distance.gif) **🔎 Interrogate it** — analyst queries against the live layers: > 🗣️ _"How many flights are over Texas right now?"_ · _"Which ships are headed to Oakland?"_ · _"What is the biggest fire near Los Angeles?"_

sources.text: # guilds.run guilds.run runs standing teams of AI agents you can inspect. A guild is a department: named roles, a shared room, shared tables. Every run keeps the prompt the model saw, every tool call, and every memory change. Agent-to-agent work opens uses of LLMs a single agent cannot cover, and it accentuates the ways those models fail. guilds.run is the framework Cigale built so that collaboration stays tractable. System thinking used to belong to people who already wrote software. With LLMs it is work anyone with a need or an interest can do, at a different level of abstraction. - **Deeply inspectable.** What the model sees is what you see. - **Deeply customizable.** Each connection, each tool, and the model for each agent is chosen for the job. - **Iterate till perfection.** A long-running multi-agent system is refined in place. - **Share the love.** Recipes carry a working guild to someone who does not want to design one from scratch. These pages are for the people who run it, the people who use it, and the people who change it. Each page describes what the code does today. The security register is the one page that keeps history. ## Philosophy - [Philosophy](philosophy.md) — why the product is shaped this way ## Getting started Three pages, in order, take an empty machine to a working guild: 1. [Install](getting-started/install.md) — requirements, the three commands, what runs, where the state lives 2. [Model keys](getting-started/model-keys.md) — the welcome dialog: a provider, its models, the default; managing keys afterwards 3. [Your first guild](getting-started/first-guild.md) — a guild, an agent, its Task, the group chat, the run, memory, a routine, a tool, a recipe Then, when the box needs it: - [Configure](getting-started/configure.md) — platform keys, and `.env`: environment integrations, reaching the box, limits, the model catalog - [Remote access](getting-started/remote-access.md) — reaching the box from another machine, with one operator or with accounts - [Operate](getting-started/operate.md) — update, back up, restore, logs, when it fails ## Concepts How the product works, for the operator. - [Users and organisations](concepts/users-and-organisations.md) — identity modes, organisations, members, the instance admin, the seed - [Guilds and agents](concepts/guilds-and-agents.md) — membership, configuration, avatars, deletion - [Prompts and memory](concepts/prompts-and-memory.md) — the system prompt, the Task, memory, hydration - [Notes and collections](concepts/notes-and-collections.md) — notes, display paths, collections, records, grants - [Runs](concepts/runs.md) — direct, group, and schedule runs; generation; sandboxes - [Group chat](concepts/group-chat.md) — tags, recipients, the cursor queue, posting - [Secrets and access](concepts/secrets-and-access.md) — secrets, grants, what reaches a sandbox - [Recipes](concepts/recipes.md) — portable guild configuration - [Prompt Studio](concepts/prompt-studio.md) — improve standing tasks on a live guild - [Guild builder](concepts/guild-builder.md) — design a recipe from a conversation - [Operator app](concepts/operator-app.md) — the screens ## Tools and connectors Native tools, the catalog, and the apps a box registers so agents can reach Gmail, Drive, and GitHub. - [Catalog](tools-and-connectors/catalog.md) — native and MCP catalogs, connections, bindings, what a run offers - [Native tools](tools-and-connectors/native.md) — notes, tables, memory, browser, scripts, routines, secrets - [Code tools](tools-and-connectors/code.md) — shell, files, search - [Connectors](tools-and-connectors/connectors.md) — token logins and remote MCP - [Gmail and Drive](tools-and-connectors/google.md) — the Google Cloud OAuth client - [GitHub](tools-and-connectors/github.md) — the GitHub App - [Registry](tools-and-connectors/registry.md) — connectors beyond the image ## Architecture For the people who change the code. - [System](architecture/system.md) — process model, topology, state on disk, images and stacks, the trust boundary - [Code map](architecture/code-map.md) — repository layout, `src/` directories, boot, the request path, the run flow - [Orchestrator](architecture/orchestrator.md) — startup and shutdown, events, PostgreSQL and migrations, codecs, the model client, the sandbox manager - [Extension points](architecture/extension-points.md) — what an edition built on core may replace - [Design system](architecture/design-system.md) — `@guildsrun/ui`: tokens, components, [Storybook](/storybook) - [Security register](architecture/security-register.md) — issues fixed and still open, with their history ## Contributing - [Contributing](CONTRIBUTING.md) — licence, pull requests, the check - [Development](contributing/development.md) — the development stack, local state and reset, verify, check, the pre-push hook, CI, fixtures - [Code guidelines](contributing/code-guidelines.md) — names, function size, scaffolding, boundaries, tests, docs ## Licence guilds.run is made and operated by Cigale AI. It is free software under the GNU Affero General Public License, version 3 only ([LICENSE](../LICENSE)). What it builds on is listed in [THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md](../THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md). The hosted edition, the layer Cigale AI runs its own service with, is separate and proprietary.
